(1) French respondents, like Americans, are able to place candidates on a feeling thermometer; (2) French respondents, as do Americans, evaluate candidates' honesty, leadership, intelligence, and likeability; and (3) French respondents, much like Americans, are willing and able to rate their own economic circumstances.

(1) French respondents are able to answer the American-style questions; (2) the answers to the American-style questions are related to the answers to the French-style questions, and to each other, in ways that are consistent with the American voting model; (3) there are some important differences between the French and the American data.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the feasibility of including ANES-type items in the French survey, and the potential for such a cross-national research design to contribute to the study of voting behaviour.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, with the exception of party identification, the French and American items are not equivalent.
French respondents are less likely than Americans to use party identification as a cue for candidate choice, but more likely to use candidate evaluations and issue proximity measures.

, in the aggregate, French respondents were more likely to express positive attitudes towards candidates, to be more critical of the President, and to be more supportive of government intervention in economic and social affairs, as well as more supportive of the left.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the French public, like its American counterparts, is not averse to responding to survey questions in the English language, and that French survey respondents are willing to answer questions in a manner similar to the way Americans answer them.
the inclusion of ANES-type measures in the French survey is feasible.
the French public is more likely to respond to the ANES-type items than is often assumed.
